You've got it exactly right. In mathematics, the fundamental difference between the two is whether the sequence of items changes the outcome.

The Core Difference

  • Permutations: Think of these as ordered arrangements. The sequence matters (e.g., a PIN code or a race podium). $ABC$ is different from $BCA$.
  • Combinations: Think of these as selections or sets. The order does not matter (e.g., picking a committee or a hand of cards). $ABC$ is the same as $BCA$.

Formulas for $n$ items chosen $r$ at a time

TypeFormulaUse Case
Permutation$$P(n, r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$Arranging trophies on a shelf.
Combination$$C(n, r) = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$$Choosing toppings for a pizza.

A simple way to remember: Permutation = Position matters; Combination = Choice only.

turns.prompt_text: so there will be many more permutations than our combinations for the same input variables
turns.response_html:
Exactly. For any set where you choose more than one item ($r > 1$), the number of permutations will always be higher because each unique group can be rearranged into many different orders.

Mathematically, the relationship is: $$P(n, r) = C(n, r) \times r!$$

Why Permutations are More Numerous

  • Combinations only care about who is in the group.
  • Permutations care about who is in the group and what order they are in.
  • For every 1 combination of 3 items (like {A, B, C}), there are $3!$ (which is $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$) permutations.

The only time they are equal is if you are choosing only one item ($r = 1$) or zero items ($r = 0$).

In a standard combination, you can only pick each item once, so your only options are {A, B}, {B, C}, and {A, C}.

If you are allowed to pick the same item twice (like {A, A}), that is a specific variation called a combination with replacement.

Standard vs. With Replacement

  • Standard Combination: You have a pool of items and once you pick one, it's gone. For "3 choose 2," there are only 3 possibilities.
  • With Replacement: You can pick "A" and then put it back to pick "A" again. For "3 choose 2," there are 6 possibilities: {A, A}, {B, B}, {C, C}, {A, B}, {B, C}, and {A, C}.

The Three Scenarios

Unlimited ReplacementUse any item up to $r$ times.{A,A}, {B,B}, {C,C}, + above

That’s an excellent way to conceptualize how these concepts overlap. Because these categories have increasing levels of flexibility (allowing order, allowing repeats), you can indeed build a "nested" or hierarchical diagram to show how the sets are related.

Conceptualizing the Nested Venn Diagram

The main confusion often comes from thinking of these as simple overlapping circles (like "A" intersect "B"). It’s better to think of them as subsets.

For your specific scenario—the base elements ${A, B, C}$ choosing 2 items—we can define four nested or related domains:

  1. Standard Combinations: (Most restrictive: No Order, No Repeats) ${A,B}, {A,C}, {B,C}$ (3 outcomes).
  2. Combinations with Repeats (Multisets): Adds items like ${A,A}$ to the standard list (6 outcomes).
  3. Standard Permutations: Standard combinations plus their mirror images (No repeats, but adds order). $AB, BA, AC, CA, BC, CB$ (6 outcomes).
  4. Permutations with Repeats: The most complete set. All standard permutations plus ordered versions of the repeated items (Order, Repeats Allowed) $AA, AB, BA, AC, CA, BB, BC, CB, CC$ (9 outcomes).

The Mathematical Problem: Visualizing Permutations with "Indistinguishable" Elements

The trick is your original input: ${A, A, B, C}$. This complicates things! This is not just choosing 2 from 3 (A, B, C); it's choosing 2 from 4, where two are the same.

In math, when we talk about permutations from a multiset ${A, A, B, C}$, we usually treat the two "A"s as "indistinguishable" from a distance (unless we label them $A_1$ and $A_2$).

If we calculate the permutations for ${A, A, B, C}$ choosing 2:

  1. We have the unique groupings: ${A,A}, {A,B}, {A,C}, {B,C}$.
  2. We find the order for each:
    • ${A,A} \to$ only $AA$ (you can swap them, but it looks the same).
    • ${A,B} \to AB, BA$
    • ${A,C} \to AC, CA$
    • ${B,C} \to BC, CB$
  3. Total "Distinct" Permutations: 7.

This is fewer than the total possibilities from the original ${A, B, C}$ set allowing unlimited repeats ($3^2 = 9$).

Why a Nested or Subset Diagram Works Best

We can show how each category of selection builds upon the previous one. We are starting from the simplest (no order, no repetition) and adding capabilities.

We can visualize this hierarchy using a subset/containment diagram rather than a traditional three-ring Venn diagram.

The diagram will show:

  • A "Permutations with Repeats" Domain: The outer circle, containing all possible arrangements ($AA, AB, AC, \dots$).
  • Nested Within it: The "Permutations" Domain: Where order matters, but we filter out cases with repeating elements ($AB, BA$, but not $AA$).
  • Separately, or Intersecting: A "Combinations" Area: This domain collects the groupings, ignoring the internal order and ignoring permutations entirely.
